In this booklet, we will watch where a patch of sunlight falls on the classroom floor over three school days. You will work with the same partner each day. Together, you will check the floor at the beginning of the morning lesson and immediately after lunch. One drawing shows where the light is once. It does not show whether that position changes. Even six drawings only show the position of the light that could be seen. They do not answer every question about why it is there.

Each time you look, mark the outline of the light on the printed floor plan and write the time beside it. A pencil and a ruler are provided. A ruler is useful for drawing a straight line. It does not make a fuzzy edge less fuzzy. If part of the outline is fuzzy, use a dotted line for that part instead of deciding the edge must be sharp. Two groups may mark the same edge differently. They should compare what they noticed before deciding whether either drawing needs to change.

Some days the light may not be visible. When that happens, write “no patch visible” in the space for that observation and leave the map itself unmarked. Do not draw where the patch was yesterday. Writing “no patch visible” counts as an observation. It does not count as a measurement of the patch’s position. The curtains will stay in their usual position, but the class will not control the clouds or record their thickness.

At the end, compare all six observation spaces with your partner. Write one sentence about a pattern you can support and one question that remains. You are not required to find a particular pattern. If too few patches were visible to establish a pattern, say so and explain which observations are missing. A careful account of what could not be observed is useful. A confident account of a patch nobody saw is not.

Welcome to the garden. Your assigned bed is marked with the number on your membership card, though a few of the painted numbers have faded. If you are unsure which plot is yours, the plan on the noticeboard is the most reliable guide, and please ask a steward before planting in any bed whose number you cannot read. Keep in mind, too, that the narrow strip beside the compost bins is planted collectively and is not an unclaimed bed.

That collective strip and the young fruit trees are cared for through the shared watering rota. The rota does not cover individual beds, even those belonging to gardeners who have signed up for rota shifts. If you will be away, you can make a separate watering arrangement with another gardener, but please add it to the noticeboard only after they have agreed—that way, an open request will not be mistaken for a job someone has already accepted.

When you need equipment, you will find the shed code on your membership card. Tools with blue handles belong to the shared collection; please return them to the shed before you leave the garden, even if you plan to come back later that evening. Tools without a blue handle may belong to another gardener and are not automatically shared. Whenever you leave the shed, please close the door so rain does not reach the lower shelves.

As you clear and tend your plot, weeds without seed heads can go into the green compost bay, while weeds with seed heads belong in the covered brown bin. If you are unsure whether a plant has set seed, leave it in the brown bin and ask at the next steward session. This is simply a sorting precaution to protect the shared compost, not a judgment on anybody's gardening.

Stewards are usually present on Saturday mornings, with the next session and any cancellations listed on the noticeboard. We are glad you are here—and please remember that we would much rather answer a small question before you plant than help move a thriving crop out of somebody else's bed.

### New in Desktop Reading Settings: Stop Image Descriptions When You Move Keyboard Focus

This desktop release introduces **Pause on Focus**, a new option in **Reading** settings that gives you more control over spoken image descriptions when navigating with a keyboard.

By default, once an image description begins speaking, it continues playing even if you move keyboard focus to another control. That remains the default behavior after updating, but you can now choose to have descriptions stop as soon as you move on.

---

#### How It Works
When you turn on **Pause on Focus** in **Reading** settings:
* **Moving focus stops playback:** Moving keyboard focus to a different control immediately stops the current image description.
* **Replaying starts from the beginning:** Moving focus back to the image will not automatically resume speech. To hear the description again from the start, use the existing **Read Description** command.
* **Your saved descriptions stay intact:** The setting does not alter the descriptions themselves. The option uses the word "pause" because stopping playback does not delete the saved description—not because playback resumes from the exact word where it stopped.

---

#### How It Works with Your Existing Description Settings
* **Automatic descriptions stay as you set them:** If you have already turned off automatic image descriptions, updating the app or enabling **Pause on Focus** will not turn them back on.
* **Works with manual descriptions, too:** Because **Pause on Focus** also stops descriptions that you trigger manually, it is still useful even if you keep automatic descriptions disabled.

---

#### Current Scope and Limitations
Keep these boundaries in mind, especially if you have more than one audio or speech source active at the same time:
* **Application speech only:** **Pause on Focus** only affects image descriptions spoken directly by the application.
* **Separate screen readers:** Speech from an external screen reader remains controlled by that screen reader, even when it is describing the same image. As a result, turning on this option will not necessarily stop all speech when focus moves.
* **Video audio:** Audio inside a video is unaffected and remains controlled by the video player.
* **Desktop only:** This option is available only in the desktop application. The mobile version keeps its existing behavior.

---

#### Reporting an Issue
If an image description continues speaking after keyboard focus has visibly moved, please let us know:
* **What to include:** Tell us the specific action you used to move focus—this is much more helpful for troubleshooting than sending the contents of the image.
* **Speech source (if known):** If you can tell whether the continuing speech came from the application or a separate screen reader, please include that detail, though you do not need to identify the source before submitting a report.

# What’s New: Introducing “Pause on Focus” (Desktop)

In our latest desktop release, we’ve added a new Reading setting called **Pause on Focus**. This option gives keyboard users more control over spoken image descriptions as they navigate.

Here is a quick guide to how the new option works, how it interacts with your existing preferences, and what to expect.

---

### What It Does

When navigating with a keyboard, spoken image descriptions have always continued playing even after you move focus away from an image to another control. 

* **The Default Behavior:** Image descriptions will continue speaking when you move focus, just as before.
* **The New Option:** Enabling **Pause on Focus** stops the application's spoken description as soon as your keyboard focus leaves the image.

#### Key Details on How It Works:
* **Why it’s called “Pause”:** We chose the name “pause” because stopping speech preserves the generated description in memory without deleting it. It does *not* mean speech will resume from the exact word where it stopped. 
* **Returning to the image:** Moving focus back to the image will not automatically resume playback.
* **Hearing the description again:** To listen to the description from the beginning, use the existing **Read Description** command. 
* **Content remains unchanged:** This setting only alters when audio playback stops; it does not change the descriptions themselves.

---

### How It Fits with Your Existing Settings

* **Automatic Descriptions Stay As You Left Them:** If you previously disabled automatic image descriptions, they remain off. Updating your app will not re-enable them.
* **Works with Manual Requests:** Pause on Focus also applies to descriptions you request manually. Even if automatic descriptions are disabled, you can still take advantage of this feature.

---

### Current Scope and Limitations

* **Desktop Only:** Pause on Focus is available exclusively on the desktop application. The mobile app continues to operate with its current behavior.
* **Application Speech vs. Screen Readers:** This setting controls only the audio spoken directly by our application. If you use a separate screen reader, that screen reader manages its own speech—even when reading the same image. Consequently, turning on Pause on Focus will not necessarily silence all active speech on your system.
* **Embedded Video Audio:** This feature does not affect audio within video players, which remains independently controlled by the player itself.

---

### Need to Report an Issue?

If an image description continues speaking after keyboard focus has visibly moved to another control, please let us know:

* **What to include:** Telling us the specific keyboard action or shortcut used to move focus is much more helpful than sending the image contents.
* **Speech source:** If you can tell whether the continued speech came from our application or a third-party screen reader, please mention it. You do not need to identify the exact source before submitting a report.

### Revised Laboratory Results

We evaluated an automated background-subtraction worksheet designed to replace manual per-sample blank entry by importing blank readings directly from the instrument log. Although eliminating manual transcription is intended to reduce entry errors that can cause discrepancies between worksheets, this comparison assessed only numerical agreement between the background-corrected fluorescence values produced by the two methods. Because the experiment did not include certified reference material, the results do not evaluate analytical accuracy against a known true concentration.

In a single session, 24 aliquots drawn from eight prepared solutions (three aliquots per solution) were measured in a fixed order by solution number. Each aliquot was measured only once, and both worksheets processed the identical set of raw instrument readings; consequently, the dataset contains no independent repeats of the instrument signal despite including three aliquots per prepared solution. A single operator, who was aware that the comparison examined data entry, completed and checked the manual worksheet before the imported worksheet was generated and therefore could not see the imported results while entering the manual values.

In the initial comparison, the reported background-corrected values agreed to the instrument's displayed precision for 21 of the 24 aliquots. The remaining three discrepancies all occurred in the final solution. Inspection of the saved instrument log showed that a single blank entry—0.2 fluorescence units higher than the blank assigned to those rows in the log—had been copied across all three rows for that solution in the manual worksheet, making the resulting manual corrected values 0.2 fluorescence units lower than the imported values. In a separate post-hoc check performed after the initial comparison, replacing that copied manual entry with the logged blank brought the corrected values for all 24 aliquots into agreement at the instrument's displayed precision.

These findings support bounded conclusions regarding calculation fidelity and transcription errors in this session. First, the complete agreement across all 24 aliquots after correcting the single manual entry provides useful evidence that the import worksheet applied the intended background subtraction to these inputs; however, this result is limited to the instrument's displayed precision and does not establish agreement at higher precision or guarantee correct blank assignment in future instrument logs. Second, while the initial three-aliquot discrepancy is consistent with a manual transcription mechanism in this session, all three differences stemmed from copying a single blank entry across three rows and thus do not represent three independent transcription errors. Moreover, because only one operator participated and knew the evaluation focused on data entry, the observed error cannot be treated as an estimate of a routine operator error rate.

Excluding instrument operation and the subsequent investigation of the discrepancy, generating the imported worksheet took four minutes, whereas manual entry and checking took eleven minutes. These timings describe only this single 24-row session under standard logging conditions; this evaluation did not measure whether the time reduction persists when instrument log formats change or when an operator must resolve a missing blank.

# Evaluation of Automated Log Import versus Manual Entry for Fluorescence Background Subtraction

### Objective and Scope
This evaluation compared two methods for background subtraction in fluorescence data processing:
1. **Manual Worksheet:** The existing workflow requiring the operator to transcribe blank readings individually for each sample.
2. **Imported Worksheet:** A proposed workflow that automatically imports blank readings directly from the instrument log to eliminate manual transcription.

The objective was to evaluate agreement between corrected values produced by each worksheet when processing identical instrument readings. This assessment is limited strictly to relative agreement between the two calculation workflows; it does not assess analytical accuracy against an absolute concentration, as certified reference materials were not evaluated.

---

### Experimental Design and Data Collection
* **Sample Structure:** Twenty-four aliquots representing eight prepared solutions (three aliquots per solution) were measured in a single analytical session.
* **Measurement Sequence:** Aliquots were measured in a fixed sequence governed by solution number. Each aliquot was measured once without duplicate instrument acquisitions; thus, the dataset does not provide independent replicates of the instrument signal.
* **Blinding and Workflow Controls:** To prevent bias during data entry, the manual worksheet was fully populated and checked before the imported worksheet was generated. The operator had no access to the imported results while entering manual data.

---

### Initial Results and Discrepancy Investigation
* **Initial Agreement:** Corrected values from the two worksheets agreed within the instrument's displayed precision for 21 of the 24 aliquots.
* **Discrepancy Identification:** The three discordant values occurred exclusively in the final solution. In the manual worksheet, a single blank reading had been copied across the three corresponding sample rows.
* **Root-Cause Analysis:** Cross-referencing the saved instrument log revealed that the manually entered blank was 0.2 fluorescence units higher than the blank value logged for those rows. Consequently, the manual corrected values were 0.2 units lower than the imported values.
* **Post-Investigation Resolution:** Substituting the logged blank value into the manual worksheet brought all 24 corrected values into complete agreement at the displayed precision. ---

### Processing Time
* **Imported Workflow:** 4 minutes.
* **Manual Workflow:** 11 minutes (entry and verification).

*Note:* These durations apply specifically to the 24-row dataset examined in this session and exclude instrument run time as well as the subsequent discrepancy investigation.

---

### Discussion and Scope of Conclusions
* **Data-Entry Error Characterization:** The observed differences are consistent with a manual transcription error in this session. However, because a single blank entry was duplicated across three rows, the three discordant aliquots reflect a single transcription event rather than three independent errors. Furthermore, because the trial involved a single operator who was aware that data entry was under evaluation, this finding cannot serve as an estimate of routine operator error rates.
* **Software Subtraction Verification:** The complete alignment of values following entry correction confirms that the import algorithm accurately performed the intended background subtraction on these inputs. This finding demonstrates computational alignment only at the instrument's displayed precision; it does not establish agreement at higher precision levels, nor does it ensure that future instrument logs will correctly assign blank values.
* **Workflow Duration:** While the automated import yielded a seven-minute reduction in processing time for this session, the evaluation did not assess whether these time savings persist when handling alternate log formats or when an operator must resolve missing blank records.

We compared two ways of subtracting background from fluorescence measurements. The current worksheet requires an operator to enter the blank reading separately for each sample, whereas the proposed worksheet imports the blank reading from the instrument log. This import is intended to reduce transcription, and removing manual entry could also affect agreement between the methods. Because the experiment did not include certified reference material, agreement here is evaluated between the two sets of corrected values, not between the worksheets and a known true concentration.

In a single session, 24 aliquots from eight prepared solutions were measured in an order fixed by solution number, with three aliquots per solution. Because each aliquot was measured once rather than duplicated, the dataset contains multiple aliquots per prepared solution but no independent repeats of the instrument signal. Both worksheets processed the same instrument readings. These timings describe this session, including its particular number of rows, and exclude both instrument operation and the later investigation of the discrepancy. ## Pilot Findings: Grate Cover Evaluation

### 1. Study Design and Measurement Protocol
The pilot examined whether installing a different grate cover would reduce the time water remained above the pavement following rain. Observations covered six drains across two streets over eight storms—four storms before the cover change and four storms afterward—yielding a complete set of 48 drain-storm observations (12 per street in each period). 

Cover allocation was non-random: crews replaced the covers on the three lower-street drains because that street had generated more prior complaints, while the three upper-street drains retained their existing covers. On the day the covers were changed, crews also cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains.

During each storm, a fixed camera at each drain recorded the number of minutes water remained visible above a painted reference line. A recorded duration of zero indicates only that water did not rise above the reference line, not an absence of runoff. Staff reported that all 48 recordings were scorable, establishing the practical feasibility of capturing the camera-based measure for these eight storms, though inter-scorer reliability (whether different raters assign identical durations) has not been tested.

### 2. Observed Measurements and Scope Limitations
Across both streets, camera records showed shorter mean durations of water above the reference line during the four storms following the intervention:

| Location | Condition | Pre-Change Mean Duration (12 observations) | Post-Change Mean Duration (12 observations) | Observed Change |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Lower Street (3 drains)** | Grate covers replaced; leaves cleared | 18 minutes | 10 minutes | −8 minutes |
| **Upper Street (3 drains)** | Existing covers retained; leaves cleared | 9 minutes | 7 minutes | −2 minutes |

These measurements reflect only the duration of visible water above the painted reference line and must be distinguished from unmeasured outcomes and parameters:
* **Drainage capacity:** Physical drainage capacity was not directly measured.
* **Peak water depth:** Peak depth was not extracted from the camera images, even though changes in peak depth could be consequential without a corresponding change in duration above the reference line.
* **Property impacts:** Flooded properties and property damage were not observed or measured.
* **Local precipitation and debris:** Neither street had a local rain gauge, no within-storm rainfall intensity data were collected, and the volume of leaves removed during the maintenance clearing was not recorded.

### 3. Unresolved Explanatory Factors
Although the mean duration fell more on the lower street (8 minutes) than on the upper street (2 minutes), this comparison does not isolate a causal effect of the replacement grate covers. Several confounding factors remain unresolved:
* **Non-random selection:** The lower street was selected because of higher complaint volume and began with a higher baseline duration (18 minutes versus 9 minutes).
* **Rainfall differences:** At the district gauge, the four post-change storms delivered less average rainfall than the four pre-change storms. Furthermore, the absence of street-level gauges and within-storm intensity data prevents accounting for localized rainfall variation.
* **Concurrent leaf removal:** All six drains were cleared of leaves on the day of the cover change. Because pre-cleaning debris levels were not measured, leaf removal cannot be assumed to explain the larger reduction on the lower street, nor can it be ruled out simply because drains on both streets were cleaned.

### 4. Utility of Current Records and Options for Follow-Up Study
The existing camera recordings remain useful for documenting conditions across the eight observed storms and demonstrating that the camera-based duration metric can be collected and scored in practice. Furthermore, the larger reduction observed on the lower street helps define questions for further investigation.

If a subsequent study is conducted to resolve the ambiguities in these findings, its design could incorporate:
* **Cover rotation:** Rotating grate covers among comparable drains to mitigate selection bias, recognizing that rotation alone will not make storm events identical.
* **Local environmental and baseline logging:** Installing street-level gauges to capture local rainfall and within-storm intensity, and measuring accumulated debris before maintenance cleaning.
* **Scoring validation and image extraction:** Testing whether independent scorers assign consistent durations to the existing or future recordings, and extracting peak water depth from the imagery if depth is of analytical interest.

# Pilot Findings: Drainage Grate Cover Evaluation

## 1. Pilot Setup and Allocation
This pilot was conducted to assess whether an alternative drainage grate cover reduces surface ponding duration—measured as the time water remains above a painted reference line on the pavement—following rain events. 

* **Observation Scope:** Observations were conducted across six drains on two streets over eight storm events: four storms prior to the cover replacement and four storms following it.
* **Cover Allocation:** Replacement covers were installed at the three drains on the lower street. The three drains on the upper street retained their existing covers.
* **Selection Process:** Allocation was not randomized. The lower street was selected for the replacement covers because municipal crews had received more drainage complaints there.

---

## 2. Observed Measurements
Ponding duration was monitored using fixed cameras positioned at each drain during each storm event. All 48 planned drain-storm observations (six drains across eight storms) were recorded and available for analysis.

* **Metric Definition:** The metric recorded was the number of minutes surface water remained above a painted pavement reference line. A recorded duration of zero indicates that water did not rise above the reference line; it does not indicate an absence of runoff reaching the drain.
* **Scoring Feasibility:** Field and analysis staff confirmed that all 48 recordings could be scored.
* **Duration Trends:**
  * **Lower Street (Replacement Covers):** The mean recorded ponding duration across 12 observations dropped from 18 minutes before the change to 10 minutes afterward (an 8-minute decrease).
  * **Upper Street (Retained Covers):** The mean recorded ponding duration across 12 observations dropped from 9 minutes before the change to 7 minutes afterward (a 2-minute decrease).
  * **Observed Comparison:** Both sets of drains showed shorter ponding durations in the second observation period, with the lower street exhibiting a greater net reduction.

---

## 3. Boundaries of the Measurement
To avoid misinterpreting the camera-based observations, the following distinctions must be maintained:

* **Ponding Duration vs. Drainage Capacity:** A decline in minutes above the painted reference line cannot be treated as a direct measurement of increased hydraulic intake or drainage conveyance capacity, neither of which was measured.
* **Duration vs. Peak Depth:** Peak water depth was not extracted from the camera footage. Variations in peak water depth could have practical significance even if duration above the line remained identical.
* **Surface Metrics vs. Property Impact:** The pilot gathered no observations regarding property damage or structural flooding. Changes in recorded ponding duration cannot be equated to reductions in flooded properties.

---

## 4. Explanations and Unresolved Variables
While the lower street experienced a greater reduction in ponding duration, this comparison alone does not isolate a grate cover effect due to several unmeasured and concurrent variables:

* **Rainfall Differences Across Periods:** According to the district gauge, the four storms in the post-replacement period delivered less rain on average than the four earlier storms. However, because no rain gauges were installed on either street, localized storm volume and within-storm rainfall intensities are unknown.
* **Concurrent Maintenance:** Maintenance crews cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains on the day the covers were replaced. The initial volume of debris at each drain was not recorded. Consequently:
  * The simultaneous cleaning cannot be dismissed as irrelevant simply because it occurred on both streets.
  * The cleaning cannot automatically explain why the lower street showed greater improvement, given the lack of baseline debris data.
* **Confounding Allocation:** Because drains were selected based on complaint frequency rather than random assignment, baseline conditions differed between streets (18 minutes baseline on the lower street versus 9 minutes on the upper street), making it impossible to attribute differential performance solely to the cover design.

---

## 5. Methodological Assessment and Proposed Follow-Up
The existing recordings provide a descriptive record of these eight storms and demonstrate that camera-based scoring of water duration above a painted line is a workable measurement technique. However, analytical and procedural questions remain unresolved:

* **Scorer Reliability:** It has not yet been evaluated whether independent scorers applying the criteria to the same video footage arrive at identical duration values.
* **Future Study Design:** 
  * A subsequent study could rotate cover types among comparable drains to improve comparative balance, although cover rotation alone cannot eliminate storm-to-storm meteorological variation.
  * Future evaluations should incorporate local street-level rain gauges to capture localized rainfall intensity and record debris accumulation levels prior to scheduled cleanings.

# Research Summary: Spoken Location Cues When Returning from a Note to a Table

When a user closes a note, our existing table view returns keyboard focus to the cell they left. Does returning focus return the user's attention to the right place? To find out whether an explicit audio landmark helps, we built a prototype version that speaks the current row label when the note closes and compared it against the existing silent focus return.

### How We Tested
Twelve experienced screen-reader users completed four tasks with the spoken cue and four tasks with the existing version. We timed only the return journey: the clock started when the participant closed the note and stopped when they activated the requested table entry. Reading the note itself sat outside the timed window.

To keep version order and table familiarity from lining up completely, six participants used the cue version first and six used the existing version first. We used different tables for the two four-task sets and reversed which table paired with which version for half of each order group. 

Did the counterbalancing eliminate practice effects? No. It prevented version and practice from overlapping completely, but it could not stop a participant from working out a search strategy during their first four tasks and carrying that habit into the second set. Our scope had two other boundaries: every participant was an experienced screen-reader user, and every prototype table fit on a single screen. We do not know how less experienced users would respond or how the cue behaves on large tables.

### What the Timings Show—and What They Do Not
For each participant, we calculated a mean completion time in each condition. Across the twelve participants, the median of those participant-level means was **38 seconds** with the cue and **41 seconds** without it. 

What does that three-second gap actually represent? It is the difference between two group medians, not the median of twelve within-person differences. Looking within individuals at the recorded precision, seven participants had a lower personal mean time with the cue, three had a higher mean, and two had equal means. We have not calculated a confidence interval or run a significance test, so these timings describe our sample rather than establish a reliable speed advantage.

### What Participants Reported
In closing interviews, nine of the twelve participants said the cue helped them feel oriented. Saying a cue feels orienting in an interview is self-reported perception, not measured navigation performance, and even among those nine users the cue carried a cost: four of them described moments when the row announcement interrupted speech they were still listening to.

The remaining three participants reported no orientation benefit. None of them asked us to remove the cue from the prototype, but should we read silence as support for turning it on by default? No. Not asking to remove a prototype feature is not the same as wanting it enabled by default, and we did not ask participants to choose a default setting.

### Implications for the Next Iteration
These observations make an orientation benefit plausible for some experienced users on short tables, while exposing a direct tradeoff: added speech competes with ongoing speech. Even if future testing shows a reliable time savings, that speech collision remains a design problem we have to solve.

One candidate for the next iteration is making the spoken cue interruptible. Would an interruptible cue preserve the orientation cue without stepping on active audio? That requires its own test. We did not build or evaluate interruptible behavior in this study, so the current timings and interview responses must not be cited as evidence for it.

# Classroom Materials Evaluation: Side-by-Side vs. Reference-Page Worksheet Diagrams

### Overview of the Comparison
This evaluation examined two versions of a single-lesson worksheet asking pupils to explain why the same amount of water appears different in a tall vessel versus a wide vessel. Both versions used identical question wording, question order, and diagrams, differing only in layout:
* **Version A (Side-by-Side Layout):** Placed the relevant diagram directly beside each question.
* **Version B (Reference-Page Layout):** Grouped the same diagrams together on a separate reference page.

Four classes completed the worksheets during a single lesson—two classes using Version A and two using Version B. Teachers selected which version their class would use before seeing any pupil responses. All teachers worked from the same written instructions, though they were free to answer pupil questions during the lesson.

---

### Sample and Scoring Procedure
Only returned worksheets were included in the analysis:
* **Version A:** 52 worksheets returned (6 additional assigned pupils were absent).
* **Version B:** 49 worksheets returned (5 additional assigned pupils were absent).

To prevent layout bias during marking, responses to the final explanation question were transcribed so the scorer could not see which worksheet version a pupil had used. Responses were scored on a two-point scale:
* **1 point** for stating that the amount of water remained unchanged.
* **1 point** for explaining that the shape of the vessel changed the water level.

To check the scoring procedure, a second scorer independently marked 10 transcribed answers. The two scorers agreed on 9 of the 10 responses and resolved the 10th through discussion before final totals were compiled. While this small check helps document how the scoring rule worked in practice, it is not a complete reliability study.

---

### Findings on the Final Explanation Question

| Score on Final Question | Version A: Side-by-Side ($n = 52$) | Version B: Reference Page ($n = 49$) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **2 points** (Both criteria met) | 31 worksheets | 27 worksheets |
| **1 point** (One criterion met) | 15 worksheets | 16 worksheets |
| **0 points** (Neither criterion met) | 6 worksheets | 6 worksheets |

In these four classes, the side-by-side layout (Version A) was associated with a somewhat higher proportion of fully credited (2-point) answers than the reference-page layout (Version B), while equal numbers of worksheets in both groups received zero points.

---

### Scope and Limitations of the Evaluation
When interpreting these results for classroom practice, several constraints of the completed evaluation apply:
* **Uncontrolled classroom and assignment factors:** Because teachers chose which version their classes used and unrecorded teacher–pupil Q&A took place during the lesson, neither pupil assignment nor teacher assistance was controlled. The evaluation cannot separate the effect of worksheet layout from existing class differences or in-lesson support.
* **No baseline measure:** No prior task was scored, so the two groups' starting knowledge before the lesson is unknown.
* **Single-question scope:** The scores reflect written responses to one explanation question rather than a comprehensive measure of pupils' general understanding of volume.
* **No pupil preference data:** Pupils were not asked which layout they preferred, so the evaluation provides no evidence on pupil preference.

Overall, this completed evaluation offers a concrete comparison of the returned responses across the four participating classes and clarifies the classroom and baseline records a more controlled evaluation would need to capture.

Two versions of a worksheet asked pupils to explain why the same amount of water looks different in a tall vessel and a wide vessel. Version A placed a diagram beside each question, while Version B placed the same diagrams together on a reference page. The wording, diagrams, and question order were otherwise identical. Four classes used the materials during a single lesson, with two classes receiving Version A and two receiving Version B. Teachers chose the version for their classes before seeing pupil responses.

Pupils returned 52 worksheets for Version A and 49 for Version B. Another six pupils assigned to A and five assigned to B were absent; the analysis included only returned worksheets. Teachers used the same written instructions, but were free to answer questions during the lesson. Those exchanges were not recorded. As a result, the comparison did not control for teacher assistance or how pupils were assigned to each version.

A scorer who could not see the worksheet layout assessed transcribed answers to the final explanation question. The scoring rule awarded one point for stating that the amount was unchanged and one point for explaining that vessel shape changed the water level. On Version A, 31 of 52 worksheets earned both points, 15 earned one point, and 6 earned zero. On Version B, 27 of 49 worksheets earned both points, 16 earned one point, and 6 earned zero. These response scores reflect a single question rather than pupils' general understanding of volume.

A second scorer marked ten transcribed answers. The two scorers agreed on nine and resolved the tenth through discussion before compiling the final totals. That check supports describing the procedure, but it is not a complete reliability study. Because the evaluation did not score an earlier baseline task, the two groups' starting knowledge is unknown.

The side-by-side layout was associated with a somewhat larger share of fully credited answers in these classes. However, the evaluation cannot separate the layout from class differences or classroom assistance. It also does not show which layout pupils preferred, because no preference question was asked. The completed work provides a concrete comparison of these returned answers and identifies what a more controlled evaluation would need to record.

As our waiting list has grown to ten households across a garden of twenty full beds, the proposed solution is to divide every returning gardener’s bed in half. It is easy to see why this seems like a fair place to begin: nobody wants access to shared land to depend on the luck of having joined years ago. Yet equal square footage is not the only thing we allocate when we assign plots. We also allocate the time and predictability required to carry a crop through its growing cycle—which is why we should divide vacant beds before dividing occupied ones.

Four full beds will become vacant at the end of this season, and dividing them will create eight half beds. Even if every offer is accepted, eight offers will leave two households on the current waiting list without a plot. That shortfall is real, and we should not speak of eight offers as though they clear the queue. What dividing vacancies first does achieve is substantial progress on the waiting list without forcing every returning gardener to uproot established plantings all at once.

Critics of this approach have argued that protecting “established planting” simply protects an established advantage. Sometimes it may, and planting a perennial certainly cannot grant anyone a permanent claim to community land. Our membership agreement promises a bed for a single season, with renewal decided annually. Because obligations in this garden are seasonal, however, major rule changes should align with the seasonal cycle rather than interrupt it without warning. I am asking for a one-season transition, not a new entitlement: returning gardeners would keep their current beds for one more season, and the committee would publish the following season’s allocation rule before annual renewals open.

Establishing the next rule before renewals open is just as important for incoming gardeners as it is for returning ones. If a new household accepts a half bed now only to learn next year that half beds will be merged or relocated, we will simply have recreated the same uncertainty on a smaller piece of ground. The rule published ahead of the next renewal cycle must therefore govern current and new members alike. While I do not yet have a preferred permanent bed size, we can commit to an orderly transition now without pretending that the permanent question has already been settled.

Just as our timeline should distinguish between an abrupt change and a planned transition, our bed count must distinguish between standard plots and accessible ones. Two of our twenty full beds are raised beds reserved for gardeners who need them, and neither is among the four becoming vacant. Because a standard ground-level half bed is not a functional substitute for a raised bed—even if both are counted the same way on a site plan—we should keep the raised beds separate from this arithmetic, leaving both the reservation and the existing access assessment unchanged.

Treating beds as real physical spaces rather than interchangeable squares on a map also requires confronting a practical drawback of starting with vacancies. All four vacant beds sit at the far end of the site, which means all eight new households would be clustered in the same area. While we could invite returning members to swap locations voluntarily, a sound proposal cannot rely on voluntary exchanges as a guaranteed fix, nor should any new member have to negotiate a private favor just to secure a usable route to a plot. Instead, the committee should inspect the paths to the eight new half beds before extending offers and report back on any access problems it cannot resolve.

When those offers go out, they should follow the current order of the waiting list. Preserving the existing queue admittedly preserves whatever disadvantages people faced in learning about the list in the first place. Reordering the list in the middle of an allocation, however, would introduce another contested rule change without prior notice—the very problem a transition is meant to avoid. A review of how we advertise the waiting list can begin immediately, alongside a commitment that any future change to how the list is ordered will be announced before it takes effect.

This remains a limited proposal with a visible cost: two waiting households may receive no offer this season. Immediately halving every occupied bed would create more places today, but only by spreading abrupt disruption across the entire garden. We should make our decision with both costs squarely in view, rather than arguing as though either the remaining queue or the established crops can be made to disappear.

### Recommendation

Approve the purchase and installation of two automatic flood-warning signs for the underpass (estimated at 18,000 units of local currency, excluding annual maintenance), **subject to three explicit conditions**:

1. **Assigned Maintenance Responsibility:** The approval decision must name a specific team responsible for monthly water-level sensor checks and allocate the necessary staff time, which has not yet been budgeted.
2. **Manual Closure Protocol:** The decision must establish a manual road-closure procedure to be used whenever the automated warning system is out of service.
3. **Drainage Project Tracking:** To prevent a visible warning device from reducing momentum on physical flood mitigation, the decision should require the next infrastructure report to state the status of the underpass drainage pipe replacement project explicitly.

The purchase should not be treated as ready for unconditional approval while staffing and backup closure arrangements remain unresolved.

---

### Rationale

#### 1. Addressing Delayed Warnings vs. Resolving Flooding
The underpass sometimes floods before maintenance crews can arrive to close the road. Automatic signs address this specific gap by providing earlier warning when water levels cross a set sensor threshold.

However, **public warning is not physical protection**. Installing signs completes a warning project, not the flood-mitigation work:
* **Warning signs (18,000 units initial estimate)** alert approaching drivers to water in the roadway but do nothing to keep water out.
* **Drainage pipe replacement (140,000 units initial estimate)** addresses the underlying drainage capacity and still requires design work.

Neither cost estimate includes annual maintenance, and there is no agreed estimate of how much either option would reduce injuries or vehicle damage. Consequently, the warning signs must be evaluated on their merits as a response to delayed road closures—not as a cheaper substitute for pipe replacement or a way to achieve the same outcome.

#### 2. Managing System Limitations
Automated warning equipment reduces risk from delayed crew arrival, and it should not be rejected simply because it cannot prevent every unsafe entry. At the same time, its operational limits explain why approval must be conditional:
* **Power and Sensor Failures:** Because sensors can fail and electronic signs require power, an unlit sign does not guarantee a clear road; it may mean the system is offline. This makes monthly sensor inspections and a manual closure fallback essential.
* **Driver Compliance:** The proposal includes a permanent static notice advising drivers that water may be present even when the electronic sign is off. While necessary, neither the permanent notice nor the active signs can prevent drivers from overlooking or disregarding warnings.

#### 3. Preserving Decision Clarity on Drainage Replacement
Approving the warning signs neither approves nor rejects the 140,000-unit drainage pipe replacement. While requiring an explicit status update in the next infrastructure report cannot guarantee that the pipe will be built, it ensures the underlying drainage problem remains formally on the agenda after the signs are installed.

The proposal therefore includes a permanent notice telling drivers that water may be present even when the electronic sign is off. This notice does not solve the problem of drivers overlooking or disregarding warnings, though warning equipment should not be rejected merely because it cannot prevent every unsafe entry.

Staff time for those checks has not yet been allocated, so it would be misleading to call the purchase ready for approval while leaving that condition implicit.

We can answer part of that concern by requiring the next infrastructure report to state the pipe project's status explicitly, though a reporting requirement cannot guarantee construction.

# Infrastructure Briefing & Recommendation

**Subject:** Proposed Installation of Automatic Warning Signs at the Flooded Underpass  
**Decision Type:** Conditional Recommendation  

---

### 1. Executive Recommendation

It is recommended that the purchase and installation of two automatic warning signs (estimated initial cost: **18,000 units of local currency**) be **approved, subject to three mandatory conditions**:

1. **Staff Allocation for Maintenance:** Formally assign a designated team responsible for conducting monthly sensor checks and allocate the required staff time before procurement.
2. **Manual Closure Protocol:** Establish a documented manual closure procedure for maintenance crews to execute whenever the automated system is unavailable due to sensor malfunction or power loss.
3. **Mandatory Drainage Status Tracking:** Require the upcoming infrastructure report to explicitly document the current planning and design status of the drainage pipe replacement project.

The purchase should not be considered ready for approval until the maintenance responsibility and closure protocols are formally established.

---

### 2. Distinction Between Warning and Physical Protection

A clear operational distinction must be maintained between alerting road users and preventing flooding:

* **Scope of the Sign Proposal:** The underpass sometimes floods before maintenance crews can arrive to close the road. Automated warning signs address this operational delay by notifying motorists sooner. They complete a **public warning project**, not a flood mitigation project.
* **Scope of the Drainage Project:** Signs do not keep water out of the underpass. Eliminating the standing water requires physical remediation—specifically replacing the drainage pipe, which remains an unresolved engineering proposal.
* **Cost Comparison:** Replacing the drainage pipe is estimated at **140,000 units of local currency**, compared to **18,000 units** for two warning signs. Neither estimate includes ongoing annual maintenance costs. The lower cost makes warning signs a smaller initial purchase, not a cheaper substitute for physical remediation. Because there are no agreed estimates for how much either option reduces vehicle damage or injuries, the two projects do not produce identical outcomes and must not be evaluated as equivalent solutions.

---

### 3. Operational Limits and System Vulnerabilities

* **System Failure Modes:** The warning signs depend on electrical power and a water-level sensor triggering at a predetermined threshold. If the sensor fails or power is cut, the signs will remain dark. A dark sign cannot be assumed to indicate a clear, safe roadway.
* **Public Advisories and Compliance:** The project includes permanent static notices informing motorists that water may be present even when the electronic signs are dark. However, warning signs and notices cannot prevent drivers from overlooking or actively disregarding alerts. 
* **Evaluation Standard:** Equipment should not be dismissed simply because it cannot prevent every unsafe entry; conversely, it cannot be deployed responsibly without human safeguards (regular testing and manual backup procedures) to manage technical failure.

---

### 4. Ongoing Governance of Drainage Remediation

* Pipe replacement remains an independent option that still requires dedicated design work. Procuring warning signs does not constitute approval, deferral, or rejection of that capital project.
* To address the risk that installing visible warning equipment will diminish public and administrative urgency to resolve the underlying drainage issue, the next infrastructure report must explicitly state the status of the pipe replacement design. 
* While a reporting requirement maintains visibility, it does not guarantee construction or project funding.

For the next set of fraction worksheets, I would like to include one worked example followed by a problem in which pupils explain a different method. At present, every example ends with a sequence of steps, and every practice problem asks pupils to repeat that sequence. While this format is efficient when the immediate aim is to practise the sequence, I am less sure that it tells us whether pupils understand why the sequence applies.

Last week's lesson highlighted this gap. After copying a worked example that used equal denominators, several pupils answered the first practice question correctly, only to add the numerators and denominators separately on the next one. Because I did not collect a starting question before the lesson, I do not know how many pupils would have made that error beforehand. Nor can I tell whether the worked example caused the error or merely exposed a misunderstanding that was already present. What I can say is that copying the steps correctly on the first practice question did not prevent the misunderstanding from appearing on the next.

To give us a clearer view of what pupils understand, the proposed explanation problem would show two correct solutions to the same addition—one using equivalent fractions and one using a diagram—and ask pupils to explain where the same quantity appears in both. It should not ask which method is always better. A diagram may be illuminating for the numbers in that question and cumbersome for others, and the worksheet should not turn a useful representation into a new compulsory routine.

Because this addition will take space on the page and time in the lesson, I would replace one of the existing repetition questions rather than add an extra page. Pupils who still need more practice with the original sequence could use the spare practice sheet we already have. That is simply a practical arrangement, not evidence that a single explanation problem will meet everyone's needs.

#### 1. Problem Statement
Currently, our final report summary lists only the runs retained to calculate the reported mean. While this keeps the mean easy to read, it obscures the batch history: a reader cannot tell whether a batch had zero exclusions or whether excluded runs were simply omitted from the summary. 

#### 2. Proposed Policy
I propose revising the report template to make exclusion decisions visible without changing how the mean is calculated or how runs are selected for exclusion:

* **Report Attempted and Retained Counts:** Alongside the reported mean in the final summary, list both the **number of runs attempted** and the **number of runs retained**.
* **Add a Separate Exclusions Table:** Include a separate table, explicitly labeled as a **Record of Exclusions**, that accounts for the exact difference between the number of runs attempted and the number retained.
* **Include Four Fields per Excluded Run (Without Raw Readings):** For each excluded run, the table would list only:
  1. Run identifier
  2. Completion status
  3. Reason for exclusion
  4. Whether a usable reading exists
* **Permit Grouped Explanations, Not Grouped Rows:** Every excluded run must appear as its own entry, and no exclusion reason should be omitted merely because it sounds repetitive. However, when the same fault affects multiple runs, the table could permit a single shared explanation for that group so long as each affected run is still listed individually.
* **Preserve Existing Rules and Raw-Data Access:** 
  * This proposal **does not** change our existing exclusion criteria, nor does it propose entering excluded readings into the reported mean.
  * Raw numeric readings for excluded runs would **not** appear in the exclusions table; they would remain in the underlying laboratory record, accessible through our existing review process.

---

#### 3. Rationale and Supporting Examples

**Exposing Rule Application Rather Than Changing the Rule**  
Our current exclusion standard already distinguishes between failed measurement conditions and unexpected results:
* *Example—Equipment Failure vs. Unusual Output:* Under our existing rule, a run stopped because a temperature controller failed is excluded because the stated measurement conditions were not met. By contrast, a completed run that produces an unusual-looking result is retained unless a separately documented equipment or handling fault justifies excluding it, because an unusual value alone does not show that measurement conditions failed. 

At present, the final summary hides how that distinction was applied to a given batch. The proposed exclusions table would not alter this rule; it would make our application of the rule visible for inspection.

**Accounting for Non-Numeric Failures Without Distorting Batch Outcomes**  
Excluding raw numeric values from the new table—and instead recording completion status, whether a usable reading exists, and the attempted-versus-retained counts—prevents two opposite distortions:
* *Example—Aborted Runs Without Readings:* When a run stops before producing any usable reading, a table limited to excluded numeric values would omit that failure entirely, making a difficult batch look cleaner than it actually was. Conversely, counting stopped runs as if they were measured outcomes would distort the batch summary in the opposite direction. 

Reporting the number attempted and the number retained beside the mean, while listing all excluded runs (with or without usable readings) in the exclusions table, captures the full operational history of the batch without conflating aborted runs with valid measurements.

---

#### 4. Unresolved Tradeoffs and Limitations

Adopting this template revision involves practical tradeoffs that the laboratory should weigh openly:

1. **Transparency vs. Risk of Unauthorized Recalculation:**  
   A central concern is that displaying failed or excluded runs will invite readers to recalculate an alternative mean from every number in sight. That risk is real and cannot be eliminated entirely. Labeling the table explicitly as a record of exclusions and keeping raw numeric readings in the underlying record (rather than in the summary table) reduces the temptation to recompute the mean and keeps the focus on the exclusion decisions themselves, though it requires reviewers who need the raw numbers to consult the underlying record.
2. **Added Reporting Time vs. Countable Batch History:**  
   Recording every excluded run and its justification takes additional staff time, especially when a single fault spoils several runs in a batch. Allowing a shared explanation for a group of runs affected by the same fault reduces repetitive prose while keeping every run countable, but the extra documentation burden remains a real cost.
3. **Inspectability vs. Substantive Judgment:**  
   Making exclusions visible improves auditability, but a fuller table cannot guarantee honest recording or fix an ambiguous rule. Reviewers will still bear the responsibility of judging whether the documented reasons for exclusion are convincing.

At present, the final summary in the report template lists only the runs used to calculate the reported mean. That is convenient for reading the mean, but it leaves a reader unable to tell whether a batch had no exclusions or whether the exclusions simply disappeared from the summary. I propose that the summary report the number of runs attempted and the number retained beside the mean, and that the template include a separate exclusions table accounting for the difference. For each excluded run, the proposed table would list the run identifier, completion status, reason for exclusion, and whether a usable reading exists. Raw readings for excluded runs would stay out of this table and remain in the underlying record, available through the existing review process.

I am not proposing that every excluded reading enter the mean, and the proposed table would expose how our existing exclusion rule was applied rather than change that rule. Our existing rule excludes a run when the stated measurement conditions were not met, and retains a completed run with an unusual result unless a separately recorded equipment or handling fault justifies exclusion. For example, a run stopped because the temperature controller failed did not meet those conditions and is excluded, whereas an unusual result in a completed run does not by itself show that the conditions failed, so that run is retained unless such a fault was recorded.

Recording completion status and whether a usable reading exists also matters when a run has no usable reading at all. A table containing only excluded numeric values would miss those failures, which could make a difficult batch look cleaner than it was. On the other hand, counting all stopped runs as if they were measured outcomes would create a different distortion. The proposed summary counts and exclusions table account for those failures without treating them as measured outcomes.

There is a concern that showing failed runs will invite readers to calculate a new mean from everything in sight. It might. We should therefore label the table as a record of exclusions and omit no reason just because it sounds repetitive. Even when a usable reading exists, adding every raw reading to that table is unnecessary for showing how the rule was applied and could make the decisions harder to see.

Reviewers will still have to judge whether the documented reasons are convincing. A fuller table cannot guarantee honest recording or repair an ambiguous rule, though it can make the decisions available for inspection. The additional reporting also takes time, especially when the same fault affects several runs. We could permit a shared explanation for that group, but each affected run should still appear in the table. That compromise would reduce repeated prose while keeping the batch's history countable.

### Proposal for Methods Meeting: Inclusion of an Exclusions Log in Analytical Report Templates

#### 3. Distinguishing the Reporting Policy from Exclusion Criteria
This proposal governs **how we document exclusions**, not **how we decide to exclude runs**. It does not alter our existing scientific criteria or admit invalid data into the reported mean:

* **The Existing Rule (Unchanged):** Measurement data are excluded only when stated experimental conditions fail due to a documented equipment, environmental, or handling fault. An unusual or unexpected numerical value alone is never grounds for exclusion.

In short, the proposed policy does not change our criteria for what belongs in the mean; it ensures that the application of those criteria is open to review.

---

#### 4. Handling Aborted Runs vs. Completed Exclusions
Accounting for both types of non-retained runs resolves two opposing reporting hazards:
* **The Hazard of Omitting Non-Numeric Failures:** If an exclusion table recorded only excluded numeric values, runs stopped before completion (such as equipment trips or operator interventions) would disappear from the record entirely. This would make an unstable or problematic batch appear deceptively clean.
* **The Hazard of Misrepresenting Incomplete Runs:** Conversely, treating aborted runs as if they were zero-value or measured outcomes would misrepresent the data. 

Requiring a dedicated status flag and an explicit accounting of the gap between "attempted" and "retained" runs ensures that the complete operational history of the batch is visible without corrupting the numerical dataset.

#### 5. Unresolved Tradeoffs and Implementation Considerations
Before adopting this policy, the committee should weigh the following tradeoffs:

Reviewers must still actively evaluate whether documented reasons are defensible; transparency facilitates oversight, but it does not replace critical scrutiny.

I propose modifying the report template to show excluded runs in a separate table alongside the final summary. Currently, the summary lists only the runs used to calculate the mean.
