A preliminary note circulated this figure as a description of respondents, but subsequent discussion sometimes treated it as an estimate for all 600 invited households.

We then approached the 240 initial nonrespondents by telephone, stopping once interviewers reached 90 completed interviews, the limit of the follow-up budget. This follow-up group was not a simple random sample of the 240 nonrespondents: participation depended both on whether a household could be reached and whether it agreed to be interviewed. Although the two-crossing persistence rule was designed to prevent transient pressure spikes from triggering valve-fault alarms, pairing a persistence requirement with a lower threshold does not, by construction alone, guarantee better false-alarm control. Because a single pressure spike need not indicate a valve fault, the persistence rule requires two threshold crossings within a machine cycle before raising an alarm, whereas the comparison rule uses a higher threshold and alarms after a single crossing. Both thresholds and the persistence requirement were fixed in advance using a separate setup recording, without reference to the evaluation recordings. While it is tempting to characterize the persistence requirement simply as a false-alarm filter, its lower threshold simultaneously alters which cycles can produce an alarm. In this bench evaluation, that parameter shift caused the persistence rule to operate not as a false-alarm reduction measure, but as a more sensitive detector—identifying more induced faults at the cost of alarming more frequently during cycles with no induced fault.

This divergence between design motivation and empirical outcome is evident in the cycle-level detection counts. The held-out bench dataset comprises 120 machine cycles recorded from a single machine—30 cycles with an induced valve fault and 90 cycles with no induced fault—where each rule can produce at most one alarm per cycle. The persistence rule raised an alarm in 24 of the 30 fault cycles and 8 of the 90 no-fault cycles, whereas the comparison rule alarmed in 21 of the 30 fault cycles and 3 of the 90 no-fault cycles. Here, "no-fault" indicates only that no valve fault was deliberately induced; the machine was not dismantled after every cycle to exclude uninduced defects. Even within that definitional boundary, the persistence rule's observed benefit in this test set was higher detection of induced faults rather than fewer alarms in designated no-fault cycles.

A secondary advantage in response speed was observed for the persistence rule, but only within strict comparative limits. Across the 18 fault cycles that triggered both rules, the mean time from logged fault onset to first alarm was 2.1 seconds for the persistence rule versus 2.8 seconds for the comparison rule. Restricting the latency calculation to these 18 shared detections avoids confounding the comparison by evaluating delays across different subsets of cycles, but it also excludes faults detected by only one rule as well as faults missed by both. Consequently, the faster mean response of the persistence rule is strictly conditional on the subset of jointly detected faults.

Taken together, these recordings characterize the tradeoff between two fixed rules on one machine under a single bench arrangement; they do not establish performance on a production line or under naturally developing faults. Because choosing between the persistence rule's higher fault detection (and faster response on shared detections) and the comparison rule's lower alarm frequency in no-fault cycles depends on the relative operational costs of missing a fault versus interrupting a cycle—neither of which was measured—no preferred rule is selected.

### Technical Evaluation: Valve Fault Detection via Single-Threshold vs. Persistence Rules

#### 1. Rule Architecture and Rationale
The persistence rule was formulated under the premise that an isolated pressure transient does not reliably signify a valve fault. To guard against transient-induced alarms, the rule mandates two threshold crossings within a single cycle prior to raising an alarm, coupled with a lower threshold value. By comparison, the baseline rule applies a higher threshold and alarms on a single crossing. All threshold parameters and the persistence requirement were determined using an independent setup recording; the evaluation set was not consulted during parameter selection. 

Although multi-crossing persistence is conceptually regarded as a false-alarm mitigation strategy, pairing it with a reduced threshold fundamentally alters cycle-level sensitivity, changing which pressure trajectories can trigger an alarm.

#### 2. Fault Detection and False-Alarm Tradeoffs
Evaluation was conducted on a held-out bench dataset consisting of 120 cycles recorded from a single machine: 30 cycles with an induced valve fault and 90 cycles with no induced fault. Here, "no-fault" signifies strictly that no fault was induced; the machine was not dismantled following each cycle to rule out unmodeled mechanical defects. Alarm generation was limited to a maximum of one alarm per cycle for each rule.

In this evaluation set:
* **Persistence Rule (Lower Threshold, Two Crossings):** Triggered an alarm in 24 of the 30 fault cycles and 8 of the 90 no-fault cycles.
* **Comparison Rule (Higher Threshold, Single Crossing):** Triggered an alarm in 21 of the 30 fault cycles and 3 of the 90 no-fault cycles.

Consequently, the persistence rule achieved higher sensitivity to induced faults (+3 cycles detected) but exhibited poorer specificity, resulting in more than double the alarm frequency across cycles designated as no-fault (8 vs. 3).

#### 3. Detection Delay on Shared Detections
Eighteen fault cycles triggered alarms under both detection methods. On this shared subset, the mean time elapsed from logged fault onset to the initial alarm was:
* **Persistence Rule:** 2.1 seconds
* **Comparison Rule:** 2.8 seconds

While restricting latency analysis to intersecting detections eliminates confounding differences between disparate cycle sets, this estimate remains strictly conditional: it excludes cycles identified by only one rule as well as fault cycles missed by both.

#### 4. Synthesis and Limits of Comparison
These findings highlight a central discrepancy between design intent and observed performance. While motivated by the suppression of transient spikes, the persistence rule's empirical benefit on this bench dataset was improved fault capture and shorter detection delays, obtained at the direct expense of elevated alarms during no-fault operation. Structuring an alarm around a lowered threshold and a persistence constraint does not, by virtue of its architecture alone, guarantee false-alarm control; it recalibrates the underlying detection tradeoff.

Finally, these results reflect two static configurations evaluated under a single bench setup with artificially induced valve faults. They do not substantiate performance across a multi-unit production environment or against progressive, naturally developing degradation. A preferred rule cannot be designated from these data alone, as the optimal operational point depends on the economic balance between cycle interruption costs and the operational risk of an undetected fault—factors that remain unquantified in this study.

We began the transcription trial by asking how complete our date entries were, which soon became a question about what we meant by completeness. The digital index has a field for a date, and filled fields are easy to count. Even so, a date in the field is not necessarily a date supported by the item itself. An empty field is no simpler to interpret: it can mean that a card has no date, that the date is illegible, or that the transcriber missed it. Counting field completion alone mixes several different kinds of work.

To separate those cases, we pulled eighty catalogue cards from a single drawer that had not yet been entered into the digital index. Two staff members transcribed each card independently. For each card, the trial instructions allowed them to enter a year, mark the date as absent, or mark it as unreadable, and did not allow them to infer a year. Afterward, a joint inspection of the cards established a reference decision for each item. This step was an internal reconciliation for the trial rather than an independent external validation of the dates.

In the reconciled record, fifty cards had a readable year, eighteen had no date, and twelve had an unreadable date. On the fifty cards with a readable year, the first transcriber entered the reference year on forty-seven and marked three as unreadable; the second entered the reference year on forty-nine and marked one as unreadable. Neither transcriber entered a year on any of the thirty cards that the reconciled record classified as absent or unreadable. Across those thirty cards, the two transcribers agreed with each other on twenty-six when choosing between absent and unreadable. We have not tabulated how often each transcriber's individual choice on that distinction matched the reconciled decision.

If we judged the index only by the share of cards containing a year, both transcribers would appear to have left a large portion of the work incomplete. That measure would ignore the cards for which the procedure required a mark other than a year, and it would hide the four cases in which the transcribers disagreed about why no year was entered. Those distinctions matter for the work that follows: a reader looking for a document's date faces a different problem from a conservator deciding whether another imaging method might help.

Because we chose the drawer for convenience, these counts describe only the trial batch and do not estimate error across the collection. They do suggest that our reporting should separate the transcription of readable years from the classification of missing or unreadable dates. Whether reporting those figures separately improves later retrieval is a further question that we have not yet tested.

**Recommendation: Object Selection for This Season’s Navigation Exhibit**

Unless the committee wishes to change the focus of this season’s navigation exhibit, we recommend acquiring the handling replica rather than borrowing the original instrument. Because the original is currently available on loan—an opportunity that may not recur—declining it can feel like a missed chance. However, availability alone cannot determine which object serves the exhibit we have designed. The choice ultimately turns on whether we want to preserve the exhibit’s current inquiry or redirect our remaining preparation time toward a different question.

As currently written, the exhibit centers on reading and error: it asks visitors to work out how a measurement changes when an instrument is tilted. That question requires physical manipulation that is only possible with the replica, since the original must remain in a sealed case. The original instrument offers a different kind of value—a material connection to its working history, including a visible maker’s correction on its scale that could anchor a compelling account of repair and adaptation. While standing beside the original provides an experience that a photograph cannot replicate for every visitor, our current text is not built around repair. Redesigning the exhibit to take advantage of that detail is possible, but doing so would require repurposing the season’s remaining preparation time.

Budget figures reinforce that this decision should rest on exhibit function rather than affordability. The loan is quoted at 18,000 units (covering transport, insurance, and a sealed case), while the handling replica is quoted at 7,000 units (including replacement parts for the season). Neither figure accounts for full staff time, and both options fit within the allocated budget. We should not frame the loan as unaffordable when the real argument for the replica is what it permits visitors to do—though the replica’s lower cost does leave resources available to test and refine the hands-on activity.

Even so, choosing the replica only makes the planned activity possible; it does not guarantee that the activity will succeed as a teaching tool. A replica’s moving parts can distract from the central question, and visitors may turn them without paying attention to the scale. Because we have not yet conducted a visitor trial, we cannot claim that handling the instrument improves understanding. 

Selecting the replica now aligns the object with the exhibit’s existing focus on reading and error while preserving the time and resources needed to trial the activity with visitors. Under this approach, we should also display a clearly labeled photograph of the original instrument and explain why a replica is used for hands-on exploration. If, instead, the committee decides that the opportunity to display the original and examine its history of repair should become the central focus of the exhibit, it should explicitly authorize that shift in direction and the corresponding reallocation of preparation time.

We recommend repeating the pond survey this season before describing this year’s lower count as a population decline. Calling for another survey before drawing conclusions can sound like asking everyone to wait, but the two recommendations work together: repeating the survey now is a practical step we can take immediately while the existing count remains too ambiguous to interpret on its own.

The current count is difficult to interpret because the survey methods changed between years. Last year’s team visited each of the eight ponds twice at dusk, whereas this year’s team visited the same ponds only once, at midday. Although fewer animals were recorded this year, the totals have not been adjusted for the reduced visit frequency or the different time of day, and the records lack the detail needed to reconstruct the missed dusk visits. To address that gap, we recommend visiting each pond twice at dusk using last year’s recording sheet. Matching last year’s schedule and recording format will make the new observations more comparable with the earlier baseline. # Position Statement: Pond Survey Methodology and Data Interpretation for the Local Advisory Meeting

### Executive Recommendation
We recommend conducting an immediate repeat survey of the eight study ponds this season before interpreting this year’s lower counts as an actual population decline. Requesting another survey is an active monitoring step to resolve a known methodological discrepancy, not a call to postpone decision-making while the current data remain difficult to interpret.

---

### 1. Survey Discrepancy: Observation vs. Population Trend
While this year’s survey recorded a lower total number of animals, this raw observation cannot be treated as a direct measure of population decline:

* **Last Year’s Protocol:** Each of the eight ponds was visited **twice at dusk**.
* **This Year’s Protocol:** The same eight ponds were visited **once at midday**.
* **Methodological Gap:** No adjustments have been made for the halved survey effort or the shift in timing, and the existing records lack the data needed to reconstruct the missed dusk visits.

A lower count is an empirical observation of what was recorded during a single midday visit; it is not, by itself, evidence of an actual population change.

---

### 2. Decision Context: Relevance vs. Causality
The observation demands attention because the advisory committee meets next month to consider a drainage proposal affecting three of the surveyed ponds:

* **Causality:** The drainage proposal cannot be the cause of the lower count, as drainage work has not yet begun.
* **Relevance:** The impending decision makes the current ecological condition of the ponds highly pertinent to the committee.
* **Timing:** An urgent timeline creates a need for reliable information, but urgency alone does not make two fundamentally different survey protocols comparable.

---

### 3. Proposed Monitoring Action and Scope
We recommend resurveying all eight ponds with **two dusk visits** using the previous year's recording sheet. 

* **What the survey achieves:** Standardizing the visit frequency, time of day, and recording method reduces a clear, avoidable procedural inconsistency and improves comparability with last year's baseline.
* **What the survey does not achieve:** It will not produce an exhaustive population census, eliminate unavoidable variables such as weather and animal detectability, or isolate the potential future impacts of drainage. 

The objective of this monitoring decision is to eliminate an unnecessary ambiguity in the evidence presented to the advisory meeting, not to settle every ecological question.

---

### 4. Contingency and Advisory Guidance
If the repeat survey cannot be completed before next month’s meeting:

1. The advisory note should present the lower observed total strictly alongside the differences in survey effort (one visit vs. two) and timing (midday vs. dusk).
2. The repeat survey should be noted as planned and pending.

The existing record justifies neither a confident claim of population decline nor an assurance of stability. A monitoring proposal should be evaluated by whether it improves the reliability of the evidence available for the pending decision, not by whether it guarantees a specific outcome in advance.

We propose revising the short discovery labels attached to twenty digitized collections where current labels repeat terms from old inventory headings without explaining whose categories those were. This proposal rests on a substantive distinction between altering a historical record and revising a discovery label. The scanned inventories are historical documents; they will remain available exactly as they are, with none of their wording removed. The proposed change concerns only the present-day catalogue text that helps a reader decide which collection to open. Even so, that discovery text is not mere packaging: it is part of how the archive represents a collection, and it shapes how readers understand the material before they open it.

Because discovery labels both guide retrieval and represent the archive's holdings, the current practice sets two legitimate routes through the material against each other. Repeating the old headings offers the real retrieval benefit of consistency: a reader following a quotation from an inventory can recognize the exact same words in the catalogue. Yet a reader who has not seen the inventory may reasonably take the discovery label to be the archive's present description of the collection. Unattributed repetition of an old heading can therefore be faithful to one route through the material while misleading on another. Because neither route is imaginary, the catalogue should not serve the first by distorting the second.

To accommodate both routes without confusing present description with the historical document, we propose replacing each single label with three elements: a current descriptive label, a note identifying the original inventory heading, and the original heading retained as a searchable alternative. This structure allows the quoted historical words to remain a working route into the collection—and leaves the scanned inventory untouched—without requiring the old heading to stand alone as the collection's present description.

One objection to revising the labels is that any replacement interprets the collection. We agree, but the existing act of choosing an inventory heading as the main catalogue label also interprets the collection, even if it looks like simple copying. Recognizing that interpretation is unavoidable on either approach is not a reason to treat every replacement as equally good. Rather, it defines the standard a revision must meet: a new label should describe the contents at the level the collection actually supports, and the accompanying note should make the relationship to the old wording visible. We have drafted labels for the twenty collections with this standard in mind, though they have not yet been reviewed by readers or subject specialists.

That commitment to making the historical relationship visible leads to a second objection: adding explanatory notes makes a short catalogue harder to scan. The proposal addresses this concern through how the elements are displayed. Search results would show the current descriptive label, while the note identifying the original heading would become visible when a reader opens the record. Preserving a scannable list of search results in this way comes with a real limitation, however, since a reader scanning search results may not see the historical wording immediately. That is a tradeoff, not a complete solution to competing needs.

Because the proposal balances competing needs rather than eliminating the tension between them—and because our drafted labels have not yet been reviewed by readers or subject specialists—its practical effects cannot be assumed in advance. We have no evidence yet that the change will improve retrieval; its purpose is to test a way of providing context while preserving a route from historical quotations. We therefore recommend a limited trial with these twenty collections, followed by checks of both successful and failed searches. Expanding the policy before that check would outrun the present case for it.

# Advisory Paper: Contextualizing Discovery Labels for Digitized Collections

### 1. Scope and Core Distinction: Discovery Labels Versus Historical Records
This proposal addresses the short discovery labels assigned to twenty digitized collections. In evaluating this change, a substantive distinction must be maintained between the archival record itself and the metadata created to index it:

* **The historical record remains unaltered:** The scanned historical inventories will remain accessible exactly as they are, with no omissions, redactions, or alterations. 
* **The proposed revision applies solely to discovery labels:** These short titles serve as the initial point of contact in the catalogue, guiding a reader’s decision on whether to open a collection. 

A discovery label cannot be dismissed as mere administrative packaging. Because it is the primary descriptive phrase presented by the catalogue, it inevitably functions as the archive’s institutional representation of the collection’s contents. Modifying a discovery label therefore changes how the archive introduces a collection, without altering a single word of the underlying historical documentation.

---

### 2. The Retrieval Dilemma: Competing Research Pathways
At present, several discovery labels reproduce terms from historic inventory headings verbatim, omitting any indication of when, why, or by whom those categories were originally formed. This practice creates an unresolved tension between two equally legitimate research needs:

1. **Citation and Inventory Tracing:** Retaining original headings offers a distinct retrieval benefit. A researcher following a direct quotation or an archival citation from an earlier inventory can locate the exact corresponding phrase in the catalogue. 
2. **Autonomous Discovery and Accurate Representation:** A reader consulting the catalogue without prior knowledge of the historical inventory is likely to interpret the uncontextualized heading as the archive’s current description of the material. 

Under current practice, fidelity to one research pathway produces distortion along the other: reproducing an old heading assists the researcher tracing historical citations, but misleads the researcher seeking an accurate description of the holdings. Both routes are real and necessary. A sound discovery system must accommodate both without conflating them.

---

### 3. Proposed Three-Part Framework
To resolve this tension without suppressing historical evidence or misrepresenting archival holdings, we propose a tripartite structure for each of the twenty collections:

* **A Current Descriptive Label:** A clear, modern descriptive title displayed as the primary entry in search results and catalogue listings.
* **An Explanatory Note:** A concise note within the collection record identifying the original inventory heading, documenting its historical vocabulary, and clarifying its relationship to the current label.
* **A Searchable Alternative Field:** The original heading indexed in the catalogue backend as an alternate search term.

Under this model, the historical wording remains an active, discoverable path into the collection: a search query using the old heading will still retrieve the record. However, those terms will no longer stand alone as the archive’s contemporary description. Search results will display the clear modern label, while the historical heading and contextual note become visible once the user opens the item record.

---

### 4. Analysis of Objections

#### Objection A: Replacement Labels Impose Subjective Interpretation
*Counter-argument:* Any descriptive label interprets the material it summarizes. Adopting an archaic inventory heading verbatim is not an act of neutrality; it is a decision to present an uncontextualized historical perspective as the institution’s current summary. Passive repetition interprets just as actively as revision.

Conceding that replacement involves interpretation does not mean all descriptions are arbitrary. A replacement label must be held to a rigorous standard: it must describe the collection strictly at the level supported by its physical contents, while the accompanying note must document the original wording transparently. 

*Current Status:* Draft labels have been prepared for the twenty collections; they must undergo formal review by readers and subject specialists before implementation.

#### Objection B: Explanatory Notes Impair Catalogue Scannability
*Counter-argument:* Placing extensive contextual prose in main catalogue listings would crowd search results and hinder rapid scanning. The proposal addresses this by confining the explanatory note to the interior of the item record.

This structure introduces an acknowledged tradeoff: a researcher browsing search results will not see the historical wording immediately. This design does not eliminate friction entirely, but balances the competing priorities of concise search-result scanning and comprehensive in-record contextualization.

---

### 5. Implementation Limits and Empirical Evaluation
We recommend a strictly bounded trial limited to the twenty designated collections. 

Because we have no prior empirical evidence that this adjustment will improve retrieval overall, the trial will be monitored through systematic checks of:
* **Successful retrieval queries:** Verifying that users locate materials using both modern descriptions and historical search terms.
* **Failed queries:** Identifying instances where searches fail or generate disorientation.

The explicit purpose of the trial is to assess whether contextual framing can be introduced without disrupting navigation from historical citations. Expanding this policy across other collections before evaluating the results would outrun the evidence and the specific case established here.

Expanding the policy before evaluating those results would outrun the present case for it.

We recommend keeping completed interviews in the weekly dashboard while ending the practice of ranking interviewers by that number alone. The count tells us whether fieldwork is moving, but it does not tell us enough to compare people whose assigned routes differ.

Some routes contain apartment buildings with a staffed entrance, while others cover scattered homes that require long walks between attempts. Moreover, assignments rotate each month, whereas the dashboard ranks interviewers each week. Monthly rotation may spread difficult routes over a longer period without making any single week's assignments comparable, though we have not estimated how large that difference is.

The ranking also leaves out work that does not produce a completed interview. For instance, a careful refusal record or a return visit at a requested time may be necessary fieldwork even when it does not result in a completed questionnaire. Including those activities in the discussion would not mean treating every attempt as equally useful; supervisors would still need to look at what happened and whether the agreed contact procedure was followed.

At the same time, we do not propose replacing the ranking with a single weighted score. We have no tested weights, and a score could conceal the same judgment inside a formula. Instead, for the next four weeks, the dashboard should show completed interviews, attempts, and route assignments together, with supervisors adding a brief explanation when discussing unusual totals.

This arrangement will take more attention than reading a league table—a cost that is part of the recommendation. While the new format may reveal problems that the old ranking missed, we cannot claim that it will improve response rates before trying it. At the end of the four weeks, the steering group should assess whether the added context usefully informed supervisory decisions and whether the burden was manageable. Our aim is to make the weekly discussion more informative while preserving a clear view of fieldwork progress.
